planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant once soil has warmed to at least 65F; seed needs light to germinate and should be surface-sown, not buried.

directions: Amrita is a vigorous Rama-type selection of holy basil originating near Amritapuri in Kerala, grown by Ayurvedic practitioners and sold by specialty medicinal-herb seed houses as a distinct named strain within the Rama tulsi group. Plants form dense, almost globe-shaped bushes with green, purple-tinged leaves and a strong, sweet-spicy aroma, flowering and branching more heavily than standard Rama tulsi. Grow it exactly as other tulsi types: pinch flower spikes regularly to prolong leaf harvest for tea, and allow a few spikes to mature late in the season for seed saving. In zones 10-12 it persists as a short-lived perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual.
sources: Strictly Medicinal Seeds — Tulsi variety descriptions

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost in cool soil; this German landrace strain is grown commercially for its flower-head yield and resin content rather than ornamental form.

directions: Erfurter Orangefarbige is a traditional German strain of pot marigold selected over generations for heavy production of resinous, deep-orange flower heads rather than for uniform double ornamental form, and it remains the strain most often recommended for home production of calendula-infused oils and salves. Press seed about a quarter inch deep into well-drained soil; plants bloom somewhat earlier and more continuously through cool weather than modern bedding-type calendula cultivars. Harvest fully open flower heads on dry mornings and dry them promptly on screens, as the sticky resin that carries much of the plant's traditional skin-soothing use is concentrated in the involucral bracts and ray florets. Deadhead routinely to keep flower production going, and allow a late flush to set seed for next year's planting.
sources: PharmaSaat (Germany) — medicinal seed catalog cultivar notes

planting.note: Best established from rooted cuttings or purchased transplants set out after all frost danger has passed; seed-grown plants of this clone are genetically variable and slower to establish, since Morita II is propagated clonally for commercial leaf production.

directions: Morita II is the Japanese-bred clonal selection of Stevia rebaudiana that became the industry-standard cultivar worldwide starting in the 1970s, prized for its favorable balance of rebaudioside A to stevioside, which gives a cleaner sweetness with less bitter aftertaste than wild-type plants. Because stevia seed is notoriously variable and slow to germinate, Morita II is normally propagated from stem cuttings, which root readily in moist potting mix under warm, humid conditions. Grow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushy growth and delay the flowering that reduces leaf sweetness. Harvest leaves for drying just before flowering, when steviol glycoside content peaks; in zones below 9, overwinter stock plants indoors or take fall cuttings to carry the clone through winter.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops — Stevia rebaudiana cultivar notes

planting.note: Surface-sow seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, as seed needs light to germinate; transplant outdoors once nights stay reliably above 50F. Germination and seedling vigor are more variable than with clonal cultivars, consistent with this strain's landrace origin.

directions: Criolla is the original Paraguayan landrace type of Stevia rebaudiana, the direct descendant of plants traditionally grown and used as a sweetener and medicinal tea herb by the Guarani people long before modern breeding produced clonal cultivars such as Morita II. It tends toward a more bitter, licorice-forward aftertaste than high-rebaudioside modern selections, but is valued by growers who want the historic, unselected form of the species or who are saving seed for further home breeding. Grow in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, keeping plants consistently but lightly watered; pinch tips to delay flowering and keep leaves at peak sweetness. Harvest and dry leaves before the plant sets its small white flowers in short-day conditions.
sources: stevia agronomy and breeding literature on landrace/'Criolla' germplasm

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in warm, well-drained soil; this named strain is grown commercially for faster root maturity than generic ashwagandha seed lots.

directions: Vedic is a named seed strain of ashwagandha offered by specialty medicinal-herb seed companies and selected for relatively quick root maturity, reaching harvestable size in roughly 100-130 days under warm conditions rather than the 150-180 days typical of unselected field-collected seed. Grow exactly as the straight species: direct sow in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, and avoid rich or constantly moist ground, which encourages leafy growth at the expense of root development. Harvest the thick, fleshy taproots in fall once the small orange-red berries inside their papery calyces begin to dry. As with all ashwagandha, the plant is in the nightshade family and the ripe berries are mildly toxic if eaten in quantity.
sources: Strictly Medicinal Seeds — Ashwagandha 'Vedic' variety description
general horticultural reference

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil; this heirloom strain is traditionally dry-farmed and performs best with minimal irrigation once established.

directions: Nagori is a named heirloom ashwagandha strain taking its name from the Nagaur district of Rajasthan, India, a traditional center of ashwagandha cultivation long regarded by Ayurvedic herb traders as producing roots of especially high quality. It is sold by specialty medicinal-seed companies as a distinct landrace selection rather than a modern breeding-program release. Grow it in lean, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in full sun with minimal supplemental water, mimicking the dry, low-input conditions of its native range, since excess moisture and fertility encourage soft top growth rather than the dense, woody taproot that is harvested. Dig roots in fall of the first growing season once the papery berry calyces begin to dry and the plant starts to decline.
sources: Grow Organic / Strictly Medicinal Seeds — heirloom 'Nagori' Ashwagandha description
general horticultural reference

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or in fall for overwintering; this registered European cultivar was bred specifically for the pharmaceutical seed trade and flowers and sets seed in its first year under long-day conditions, unlike strictly biennial wild milk thistle.

directions: Sylbina is a European-registered milk thistle cultivar selected for elevated silymarin content in its seed, the flavonolignan complex that is the basis of milk thistle's traditional and continued use in liver-support preparations. Direct sow seed about a half inch deep into well-drained soil; established plants tolerate drought and poor soil but need full sun to develop the large, spiny, white-marbled rosettes and tall flowering stalks typical of the species. Allow the purple thistle flower heads to dry fully on the plant before cutting and threshing them to collect seed, wearing gloves to handle the sharp spines. Because this is a seed-propagated agricultural cultivar rather than a clone, some variability between plants in a given packet is normal.
sources: European milk-thistle breeding literature on registered high-silymarin cultivars

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring; this Hungarian-bred cultivar is grown commercially across central Europe for seed yield and silymarin content under field conditions, including drought-prone sites.

directions: Budakalaszi is a named Hungarian milk thistle cultivar developed for commercial seed and silymarin production and studied extensively in European agronomic trials, including under drought stress, where it has shown good tolerance of lean, dry growing conditions. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun; plants form the same large spiny, white-veined rosette as other milk thistle before sending up tall branching flower stalks topped with purple thistle blooms. Water sparingly once established, since this cultivar was specifically bred and tested for reliable seed yield under reduced irrigation. Harvest seed heads once they turn from green to brown and the bristly pappus begins to loosen, then dry and thresh to collect the seed.
sources: European agronomic research on Silybum marianum cv. Budakalaszi
general horticultural reference

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; seed needs light to germinate, so press into the soil surface rather than burying. This tetraploid Slovak-registered strain was bred for larger flowers and a richer essential oil yield than standard diploid chamomile.

directions: Lutea is a tetraploid German chamomile cultivar first registered in Slovakia and valued for an essential oil unusually rich in alpha-bisabolol, the soothing compound most associated with chamomile's traditional use in teas and skin preparations. Its flowers and plants both run larger than standard diploid German chamomile, making hand or mechanical harvest somewhat more efficient. Surface-sow seed in cool, moist soil in early spring, since seed needs light to germinate; thin seedlings to stand several inches apart in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Harvest the daisy-like flower heads as the white ray petals begin to droop downward, which is when essential oil content peaks, and dry them quickly out of direct sun to preserve color and aroma.
sources: Slovak Central Control and Testing Institute in Agriculture — 'Lutea' cultivar registration

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors around the last frost; this Polish-bred open-pollinated cultivar is grown commercially for root weight and essential oil content and is typically harvested at the end of its first full growing season.

directions: Lubelski is a Polish open-pollinated valerian cultivar bred for larger, heavier roots and higher essential oil content than wild-collected or unselected garden valerian, and it remains a standard cultivated variety in the Central European valerian root industry. Sow seed shallowly in consistently moist, fertile soil; germination can be slow and uneven, so patience is needed. Plants form a basal rosette the first year and send up tall, hollow flower stalks topped with clusters of small pink-white, sweetly fragrant flowers in their second year or in a favorable first year. Roots are dug for drying in fall once the characteristic strong aroma develops fully, typically at the end of the first full season of growth for this high-yielding strain.
sources: Polish agronomic literature on cultivated 'Lubelski' valerian

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors around the last frost into consistently moist, fertile soil; this German-bred ('Artener Zuchtung') selection is grown commercially for uniform, high-yielding roots.

directions: Anthos (also known by its German breeding name 'Artener Zuchtung') is a selected valerian strain grown for more uniform plant habit and higher root yield than common garden-strain valerian, with roots noted for elevated levels of the essential oils and valepotriates associated with the plant's traditional calming reputation. Culture is the same as other valerian: sow into rich, evenly moist soil and keep seedlings consistently watered through their first season, as valerian does not tolerate drying out while establishing. Plants form a clump of deeply cut leaves topped by tall stems of small, fragrant pink-white flowers that draw abundant pollinators. Dig roots for drying in fall, when their characteristically strong, musky aroma is most pronounced, cutting back top growth first to make the fibrous root mass easier to lift.
sources: European valerian cultivation literature on 'Anthos' / 'Artener Zuchtung'

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow, as seed needs light to germinate. This open-pollinated strain is maintained for single, daisy-type flowers rather than the double or variegated forms grown mainly for ornament.

directions: This single-flowered strain of feverfew is maintained by medicinal-herb seed growers specifically as a non-double, non-variegated line selected for consistent parthenolide content, the compound most associated with feverfew's traditional use for headache relief, rather than for the showier double pompom or golden-leaved forms bred as garden ornamentals. Plants are otherwise grown like any feverfew: start seed indoors and transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun, where it quickly forms a bushy clump of aromatic, finely divided leaves topped by small white-and-yellow daisy flowers. Harvest leaves (and flowering tops, if desired) for drying just as the plant comes into bloom, when the active compounds are most concentrated. Deadhead to extend bloom, or allow some flowers to set seed, since feverfew self-sows readily and can naturalize in the garden.
sources: Thyme Garden Herb Seeds — Feverfew, Single Flower variety description
